claims.evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about Xenopus lateral line anatomy and function.

claims.claim: In many other vertebrates, the lateral line system has an electrosensory division.
claims.source: However, in many other vertebrates, the lateral line system also has an electrosensory division (Bullock et al., 1983; Baker et al., 2013; Crampton, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreception.

claims.claim: In electroreceptive non-teleost jawed vertebrates, some or all of the neuromast lines on the head are flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors.
claims.source: In electroreceptive non-teleost jawed vertebrates, some or all of the neuromast lines on the head are flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors, which respond to weak cathodal stimuli such as the electric fields surrounding other animals in water (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Crampton, 2019; Leitch and Julius, 2019; Chagnaud et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreceptor anatomy and distribution.

claims.claim: Electroreceptors respond to weak cathodal stimuli such as the electric fields surrounding other animals in water.
claims.source: In electroreceptive non-teleost jawed vertebrates, some or all of the neuromast lines on the head are flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors, which respond to weak cathodal stimuli such as the electric fields surrounding other animals in water (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Crampton, 2019; Leitch and Julius, 2019; Chagnaud et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreceptor function.

claims.claim: Electroreception is mediated by voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane.
claims.source: Electroreception is mediated by voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Leitch and Julius, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreceptor physiology.

claims.claim: The voltage sensor in cartilaginous fishes was recently identified as the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3.
claims.source: The voltage sensor was recently identified in cartilaginous fishes as the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 (Bellono et al., 2017; Bellono et al., 2018), whose pore-forming alpha subunit is encoded by Cacna1d.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent research identifying the voltage sensor in electroreceptors.

claims.claim: The pore-forming alpha subunit of Cav1.3 is encoded by Cacna1d.
claims.source: The voltage sensor was recently identified in cartilaginous fishes as the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 (Bellono et al., 2017; Bellono et al., 2018), whose pore-forming alpha subunit is encoded by Cacna1d.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the molecular composition of Cav1.3 channels.

claims.claim: Cav1.3 is required for synaptic transmission at hair-cell ribbon synapses.
claims.source: Cav1.3 is also required for synaptic transmission at hair-cell ribbon synapses (Moser et al., 2020; Mukhopadhyay and Pangrsic, 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on hair cell synaptic function.

claims.claim: Electroreceptors, like hair cells, have an apical primary cilium and basolateral ribbon synapses with lateral line afferents.
claims.source: Electroreceptors, like hair cells, have an apical primary cilium and basolateral ribbon synapses with lateral line afferents (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing the ultrastructure of electroreceptors and hair cells.

claims.claim: Hair cells have a highly ordered, stepped array of apical microvilli ('stereocilia') that forms the 'hair bundle' critical for hair-cell mechanotransduction.
claims.source: However, in contrast to the highly ordered, stepped array of apical microvilli ('stereocilia') that forms the 'hair bundle' critical for hair-cell mechanotransduction (Caprara and Peng, 2022), electroreceptors in many species (for example, cartilaginous fishes; ray-finned paddlefishes and sturgeons) lack apical microvilli altogether (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on hair cell structure and function.

claims.claim: Electroreceptors in many species (for example, cartilaginous fishes; ray-finned paddlefishes and sturgeons) lack apical microvilli altogether.
claims.source: However, in contrast to the highly ordered, stepped array of apical microvilli ('stereocilia') that forms the 'hair bundle' critical for hair-cell mechanotransduction (Caprara and Peng, 2022), electroreceptors in many species (for example, cartilaginous fishes; ray-finned paddlefishes and sturgeons) lack apical microvilli altogether (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing electroreceptor ultrastructure in different species.

claims.claim: Electroreceptors in some species have a few apical microvilli.
claims.source: Electroreceptors in other species have a few apical microvilli, while the electroreceptors of the amphibian axolotl have around 200 microvilli surrounding an eccentrically positioned primary cilium (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing electroreceptor ultrastructure in different species.

claims.claim: The electroreceptors of the amphibian axolotl have around 200 microvilli surrounding an eccentrically positioned primary cilium.
claims.source: Electroreceptors in other species have a few apical microvilli, while the electroreceptors of the amphibian axolotl have around 200 microvilli surrounding an eccentrically positioned primary cilium (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing axolotl electroreceptor ultrastructure.

claims.claim: Axolotl electroreceptors were described as 'remarkably similar to immature hair cells'.
claims.source: Indeed, axolotl electroreceptors were described as "remarkably similar to immature hair cells" (Northcutt et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This statement is a direct quote from a cited publication.

claims.claim: The apical surface of electroreceptors varies considerably across different vertebrate groups.
claims.source: Thus, despite their shared function, the apical surface of electroreceptors (where voltage-sensing occurs; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Leitch and Julius, 2019) varies considerably across different vertebrate groups.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the described variation in electroreceptor ultrastructure across species.

claims.claim: Voltage-sensing in electroreceptors occurs at the apical surface.
claims.source: Thus, despite their shared function, the apical surface of electroreceptors (where voltage-sensing occurs; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Leitch and Julius, 2019) varies considerably across different vertebrate groups.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature on electroreceptor physiology.

claims.claim: Fate-mapping experiments have shown that neuromasts, ampullary organs (where present) and their afferent neurons all develop from a series of pre-otic and post-otic lateral line placodes on the embryonic head.
claims.source: Fate-mapping experiments have shown that neuromasts, ampullary organs (where present) and their afferent neurons all develop from a series of pre-otic and post-otic lateral line placodes on the embryonic head (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to fate-mapping studies.

claims.claim: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment.
claims.source: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment: neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each ridge, and ampullary organs (if present) form later, in fields on the flanks of the ridge (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to developmental studies of the lateral line system.

claims.claim: Neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each sensory ridge.
claims.source: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment: neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each ridge, and ampullary organs (if present) form later, in fields on the flanks of the ridge (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to developmental studies of the lateral line system.

claims.claim: Ampullary organs form later, in fields on the flanks of the sensory ridge.
claims.source: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment: neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each ridge, and ampullary organs (if present) form later, in fields on the flanks of the ridge (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to developmental studies of the lateral line system.

claims.claim: A variety of genes are expressed in developing ampullary organs as well as neuromasts in embryos from cartilaginous fishes, lobe-finned bony fishes/tetrapods, and ray-finned bony fishes.
claims.source: This enabled us to identify a variety of genes expressed in developing ampullary organs as well as neuromasts, in embryos from the three major jawed-vertebrate groups, that is, cartilaginous fishes (lesser-spotted catshark, Scyliorhinus canicula, and little skate, Leucoraja erinacea; O'Neill et al., 2007; Gillis et al., 2012); lobe-finned bony fishes/tetrapods (a urodele amphibian, the axolotl, Ambystoma mexicanum; Modrell and Baker, 2012); and ray-finned bony fishes (a chondrostean, the Mississippi paddlefish, Polyodon spathula; Modrell et al., 2011a; Modrell et al., 2011b; Modrell et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous gene expression studies by the authors.

claims.claim: Differential bulk RNA-seq in late-larval paddlefish yielded a dataset of almost 500 genes that were putatively enriched in lateral line organs.
claims.source: We also took an unbiased discovery approach using differential bulk RNA-seq in late-larval paddlefish, which yielded a dataset of almost 500 genes that were putatively enriched in lateral line organs (Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous RNA-seq study by the authors.

claims.claim: Validation by in situ hybridisation of a subset of candidates from the RNA-seq dataset suggested that conserved molecular mechanisms were involved in hair cell and electroreceptor development.
claims.source: Validation by in situ hybridisation (ISH) of a subset of candidates from this dataset suggested that conserved molecular mechanisms were involved in hair cell and electroreceptor development, and that hair cells and electroreceptors were closely related physiologically (Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from gene expression validation studies cited in the text.

claims.claim: Hair cells and electroreceptors are closely related physiologically.
claims.source: Validation by in situ hybridisation (ISH) of a subset of candidates from this dataset suggested that conserved molecular mechanisms were involved in hair cell and electroreceptor development, and that hair cells and electroreceptors were closely related physiologically (Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from gene expression validation studies cited in the text.

claims.claim: Developing ampullary organs express the key 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1 and Pou4f3.
claims.source: For example, developing ampullary organs express the key 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1 and Pou4f3 (see Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021), and genes essential for the function of hair cell ribbon synapses, including the voltage-gated calcium channel gene Cacna1d, encoding Cav1.3 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to gene expression studies.

claims.claim: Developing ampullary organs express genes essential for the function of hair cell ribbon synapses, including Cacna1d.
claims.source: For example, developing ampullary organs express the key 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1 and Pou4f3 (see Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021), and genes essential for the function of hair cell ribbon synapses, including the voltage-gated calcium channel gene Cacna1d, encoding Cav1.3 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to gene expression studies.

claims.claim: Two electroreceptor-specific voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes (Kcna5 and Kcnab3) are expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
claims.source: We also identified a handful of genes expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts, including two electroreceptor-specific voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes (Kcna5 and Kcnab3) and a single transcription factor gene, Neurod4 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous gene expression study by the authors.

claims.claim: Neurod4 is a transcription factor gene expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
claims.source: We also identified a handful of genes expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts, including two electroreceptor-specific voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes (Kcna5 and Kcnab3) and a single transcription factor gene, Neurod4 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous gene expression study by the authors.

claims.claim: Fifteen transcription factor genes have shared expression in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
claims.source: Up to that point, we had reported the shared expression of fifteen transcription factor genes in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, but only one transcription factor gene with restricted expression, namely, electrosensory-restricted Neurod4 (Modrell et al., 2011a; Modrell et al., 2011b; Modrell et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous gene expression studies by the authors.

claims.claim: 23 more transcription factor genes were identified as expressed within developing lateral line organs in paddlefish and/or sterlet.
claims.source: More recently (Minařík et al., 2024), we used the late-larval paddlefish lateral line organ-enriched dataset (Modrell et al., 2017a), as well as a candidate gene approach, to identify 23 more transcription factor genes expressed within developing lateral line organs in paddlefish and/or in a related, more experimentally tractable chondrostean, the sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus, a small sturgeon; for example, Chen et al., 2018; Baloch et al., 2019; Stundl et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claims.claim: Twelve transcription factor genes including Gfi1 are expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
claims.source: Twelve of these transcription factor genes—including Gfi1—were expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Minařík et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claims.claim: Developing ampullary organs and neuromasts express the three 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1.
claims.source: Thus, developing ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, express the three 'hair cell' transcription factor genes—Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1—whose co-expression is sufficient to drive postnatal mouse cochlear supporting cells to adopt a 'hair cell-like' fate, albeit not to form fully mature hair cells (Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Iyer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to gene expression studies and functional studies in mouse.

claims.claim: Co-expression of Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1 is sufficient to drive postnatal mouse cochlear supporting cells to adopt a 'hair cell-like' fate, albeit not to form fully mature hair cells.
claims.source: Thus, developing ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, express the three 'hair cell' transcription factor genes—Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1—whose co-expression is sufficient to drive postnatal mouse cochlear supporting cells to adopt a 'hair cell-like' fate, albeit not to form fully mature hair cells (Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Iyer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to functional studies in mouse.

claims.claim: Six novel ampullary organ-restricted transcription factor genes were identified.
claims.source: We also identified six novel ampullary organ-restricted transcription factor genes and the first-reported mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes (Minařík et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claims.claim: The first-reported mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes were identified.
claims.source: We also identified six novel ampullary organ-restricted transcription factor genes and the first-reported mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes (Minařík et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claims.claim: Foxg1 is one of five mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes.
claims.source: One of the five mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes was Foxg1, which was expressed and maintained in the central region of sensory ridges where lines of neuromasts form, although excluded from hair cells (Minařík et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claims.claim: Foxg1 is expressed and maintained in the central region of sensory ridges where lines of neuromasts form, although excluded from hair cells.
claims.source: One of the five mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes was Foxg1, which was expressed and maintained in the central region of sensory ridges where lines of neuromasts form, although excluded from hair cells (Minařík et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors showing gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: Targeting Foxg1 resulted in the ectopic formation of ampullary organs within neuromast lines.
claims.source: Targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 resulted in a striking phenotype: the ectopic formation of ampullary organs within neuromast lines, and in some cases the fusion of ampullary organ fields that normally develop either side of a line of neuromasts.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis showing ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants.

claims.claim: Targeting Foxg1 resulted in the fusion of ampullary organ fields that normally develop either side of a line of neuromasts in some cases.
claims.source: Targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 resulted in a striking phenotype: the ectopic formation of ampullary organs within neuromast lines, and in some cases the fusion of ampullary organ fields that normally develop either side of a line of neuromasts.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis showing fusion of ampullary organ fields in Foxg1 crispants.

claims.claim: Sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically in Foxg1 crispants.
claims.source: In addition, sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically, supporting a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development, as recently reported in zebrafish (Bell et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis showing missing neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants.

claims.claim: The missing neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants support a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development.
claims.source: In addition, sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically, supporting a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development, as recently reported in zebrafish (Bell et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of missing neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants, supported by a citation to a recent zebrafish study.

claims.claim: FoxG1 has a direct role in neuromast development in zebrafish.
claims.source: In addition, sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically, supporting a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development, as recently reported in zebrafish (Bell et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent zebrafish study.

claims.claim: The presence of ectopic ampullary organs within neuromast lines in Foxg1 crispants suggests that ampullary organs may be the 'default' developmental fate for lateral line sensory ridges.
claims.source: However, the presence of ectopic ampullary organs within neuromast lines in Foxg1 crispants suggests the unexpected but intriguing hypothesis that ampullary organs may be the 'default' developmental fate for lateral line sensory ridges, and that this is repressed by FoxG1, allowing neuromasts to form instead.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental observation of ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants.

claims.claim: FoxG1 represses the default ampullary organ fate, allowing neuromasts to form instead.
claims.source: However, the presence of ectopic ampullary organs within neuromast lines in Foxg1 crispants suggests the unexpected but intriguing hypothesis that ampullary organs may be the 'default' developmental fate for lateral line sensory ridges, and that this is repressed by FoxG1, allowing neuromasts to form instead.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental observation of ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants.

claims.claim: Sox2 is a supporting cell marker in sterlet lateral line organs.

claims.claim: Sox2 shows strong expression in neuromasts and much weaker expression in ampullary organs at stage 45 in sterlet.

claims.claim: Cacna1d shows expression in neuromasts and ampullary organs at stage 45 in sterlet.
claims.source: In situ hybridisation (ISH) for the hair cell and electroreceptor marker Cacna1d at stage 45 shows expression in neuromasts and ampullary organs.

claims.claim: The most efficient results for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in sterlet were obtained by injecting 1-cell embryos with a preassembled mix of Cas9 protein plus two chemically modified sgRNAs.

claims.claim: The optimum temperature for maintaining sterlet embryos for normal development is 16°C.

results.result: Atoh1 is required for both hair cell and electroreceptor differentiation in sterlet, and for expression of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 in both neuromasts and ampullary organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C90-C92, C94-C95, C97-C99, C108-C109 collectively demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of Atoh1 results in mosaic loss of Cacna1d, Kcnab3, Pou4f3, and Gfi1 expression in both neuromasts and ampullary organs (59-87% of crispants showed phenotypes), while Sox2-positive supporting cells remain present. The data show that Atoh1 is required for both hair cell and electroreceptor differentiation and lies upstream of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 in both organ types. The phenotypes are well-documented with quantitative data across multiple markers and independent batches.

results.result: Targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 resulted in ectopic ampullary organs forming within neuromast lines and gaps where neuromasts are missing, suggesting FoxG1 represses ampullary organ/electroreceptor formation and is necessary for neuromast formation/maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C55-C57, C127-C134, C137-C140, C159-C161 demonstrate that Foxg1 disruption leads to two distinct phenotypes: (1) ectopic ampullary organs within neuromast lines (44-63% of crispants depending on marker), including fusion of ampullary organ fields and electroreceptors within neuromasts (13% of phenotypic crispants), and (2) gaps in neuromast lines (55% of crispants). The data are supported by multiple markers (Cacna1d, Kcnab3, Mafa, Neurod4) across independent batches with successful genotyping confirmation. The dual phenotype supports both a role in neuromast formation/maintenance and repression of electrosensory fate.

results.result: Targeting ampullary organ-restricted Neurod4 did not yield any phenotype, potentially due to redundancy with other Neurod family members (Neurod1 and Neurod6) expressed in sterlet ampullary organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C112-C113, C117, C119-C122 show that despite successful disruption of Neurod4 (confirmed by genotyping), no phenotype was observed in 48 crispants across multiple markers (Kcnab3, Cacna1d). The authors provide a plausible explanation supported by new gene expression data showing Neurod1 and Neurod6 are co-expressed in ampullary organs (C119), suggesting functional redundancy. The negative result is well-documented and the redundancy hypothesis is supported by expression data, though functional testing of multiple Neurod genes would be needed to confirm this explanation.

results.result: The data support conservation of developmental mechanisms between hair cells and electroreceptors, including the Atoh1-Pou4f3 feed-forward circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C7, C40-C41, C165-C166, C168 represent inferences drawn from the experimental results showing shared gene expression and functional requirements. The conservation is supported by: (1) extensive shared gene expression between neuromasts and ampullary organs (C3, C40), (2) Atoh1 requirement for both cell types (C7, C165), and (3) Atoh1 requirement for Pou4f3 and Gfi1 expression in both organs (C166). These data collectively support the hypothesis that electroreceptors evolved as a transcriptionally related 'sister cell type' to hair cells (C168), though this remains an evolutionary inference rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: The authors speculate that electrosensory organs may be the 'default' developmental fate of lateral line primordia in electroreceptive vertebrates, with FoxG1 repressing this fate to allow neuromast formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C60-C61 represent a speculative hypothesis based on the Foxg1 phenotype. While the observation of ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants is well-supported, the 'default fate' hypothesis is one of multiple possible explanations (as acknowledged in C183-C185). The authors appropriately present this as speculation, but alternative mechanisms (indirect effects via loss of inhibitory signals from neuromasts, C184) are equally plausible. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish between direct repression versus indirect effects.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in sterlet was optimized, with the most efficient results obtained by injecting 1-cell embryos with preassembled Cas9 protein plus two chemically modified sgRNAs and maintaining embryos at room temperature for ~6 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 describe the optimized CRISPR protocol that yielded 56.8% efficiency for Tyr targeting. The protocol details are clearly described and the efficiency is quantified. The biological rationale (holoblastic cleavage timing, temperature requirements) is provided. This represents a methodological advance for working with sterlet embryos.

results.result: Analysis of the sterlet reference genome revealed that ohnologs for Tyr, Atoh1, Neurod4, and Foxg1 have been retained with high sequence identity, and the sgRNAs used target both ohnologs with minimal or no mismatches.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79, C84-C89, C114-C116, C124-C126 provide genomic analysis showing retention of ohnologs for all targeted genes with 84-99% amino acid identity. The sgRNA targeting analysis is thorough, addressing potential mismatches and their likely impact on targeting efficiency based on position and cited literature (C87). This analysis is important for interpreting the functional results in the context of the sterlet's tetraploid genome, though the authors acknowledge they could not always confirm disruption of both ohnologs through genotyping.

results.result: Quantitative phenotypic analysis of Atoh1 crispants showed that 67% had mosaic loss of hair cells/electroreceptors, with 77% showing bilateral phenotypes and 78% of phenotypic sides classified as severe.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C107 provide detailed quantitative phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants. The data show clear patterns of mosaicism consistent with CRISPR editing in holoblastically cleaving embryos. The severity scoring (severe/moderate/mild based on proportion of organs affected) is clearly defined and quantified. This detailed phenotypic characterization strengthens the main findings about Atoh1 function.

results.result: Quantitative phenotypic analysis of Foxg1 crispants showed that 64% had phenotypes, with different neuromast lines showing distinct patterns of disruption: the otic line was most commonly affected (76%) primarily by gaps (88%), while the preopercular line was least affected (26%) primarily by ectopic ampullary organs (95%).
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C158 provide extensive quantitative phenotypic scoring of Foxg1 crispants across four neuromast lines. The data reveal line-specific patterns that correlate with ampullary organ field size (C158), suggesting biological significance. The detailed scoring (including severity, type of disruption, and laterality) is well-documented in supplementary files. This comprehensive phenotypic characterization supports the main conclusions about Foxg1 function and provides insights into regional differences in lateral line development.

results.result: Gene expression analysis in sterlet at stage 45 established marker expression patterns: Sox2 (supporting cells, strong in neuromasts, weak in ampullary organs), Cacna1d (hair cells and electroreceptors), Kcnab3 (electroreceptors only), Atoh1 (ampullary organs and weakly in neuromasts), Neurod4 (ampullary organs only), and Foxg1 (neuromast lines, excluded from hair cells).
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C70 describe baseline gene expression patterns that serve as reference for interpreting the CRISPR phenotypes. The expression patterns are documented by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1. These expression patterns are consistent with previous studies cited by the authors and provide essential context for the functional experiments.

results.result: Analysis of the sterlet genome showed that approximately 70% of ohnologs from a whole-genome duplication have been retained, suggesting a high level of functional tetraploidy, contrasting with earlier microsatellite data suggesting functional diploidy.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 cite published genome analysis (Du et al., 2020) showing retention of ~70% of ohnologs and functional tetraploidy. This contextualizes the experimental design and interpretation, as the authors needed to consider potential redundancy between ohnologs. The contrast with earlier microsatellite data (C74) highlights the evolution of understanding about sterlet genome organization.

results.result: Background information on lateral line anatomy, electroreceptor structure and function, and developmental origins from lateral line placodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C13-C37 provide established background knowledge about lateral line systems, electroreceptor structure/function, and development, supported by appropriate citations to the literature. This background contextualizes the experimental work but does not represent new findings from this study.

results.result: Previous work by the authors identified genes expressed in developing lateral line organs across multiple species, including shared expression of 'hair cell' transcription factors in ampullary organs and identification of mechanosensory-restricted and electrosensory-restricted transcription factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C42-C54 summarize the authors' previous gene expression studies that motivated the current functional work. These claims are supported by citations to the authors' prior publications and provide essential context for gene selection in the CRISPR experiments. The previous identification of Foxg1 as mechanosensory-restricted (C53-C54) directly motivated its functional testing in this study.

results.result: Literature context on Atoh1 and Foxg1 function in other systems, including zebrafish lateral line, mouse inner ear, and the Atoh1-Pou4f3 feed-forward circuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C164, C169-C173, C193-C194 provide literature context from other model systems that informs interpretation of the sterlet results. These are appropriately cited and provide comparative context, particularly for Atoh1 function in zebrafish (C162) and Foxg1 function in mouse inner ear (C170-C173), which help interpret the sterlet phenotypes.

results.result: Sterlet eggs are large (~2.5 mm diameter), undergo holoblastic cleavage, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos has been reported.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 provide basic biological information about sterlet embryology and note that CRISPR in sterlet has been reported (including by two co-authors). This contextualizes the methodological approach and acknowledges prior work, though the current study represents optimization and application to new genes.
